title: Stress, Burnout & Psychological Demands
description: Explore a busy week versus chronic overload through dialogue, evidence and psychological reasoning.

lessons.title: When rest doesn't fix the workload
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of a busy week versus chronic overload.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
A job-demands and resources formulation asks whether the work can be done with the time and staffing actually available. Working through breaks may temporarily reduce a backlog while hiding an unsustainable workload. Burnout concerns chronic occupational stress that has not been successfully managed, rather than an isolated busy period.

Fatigue can reflect other health or life factors. A full account needs the duration of demands and how work is affecting functioning.
nodes.sources: WHO, Burn-out: an occupational phenomenon; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands-Resources model.

nodes.title: Try a different response
nodes.prompt: The goal is to improve the situation without pretending that you can read the person's mind.
nodes.explanation: A proportionate response deals with the actual situation: Document the workload against available hours and ask which duties will be reduced or resourced. Its value does not depend on the other person accepting an interpretation of their motives.
nodes.counterexample: Some situations require independent support or safer channels rather than another direct conversation. Fatigue can reflect other health or life factors. A full account needs the duration of demands and how work is affecting functioning.
nodes.sources: WHO, Burn-out: an occupational phenomenon; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands-Resources model.

lessons.title: What would change your mind?
lessons.teach: An initial explanation is useful only if it can be challenged. Revisit the characters, test a rival account and apply the idea in another setting. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Test an account of a busy week versus chronic overload with new evidence and transfer it to a new case.
